narrative:
The model predicted an 84.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three academic performance signals. The single most important factor was your class ranking at the end of your third year. Placing in the bottom decile of your class sent a strong signal toward future bar exam difficulty. Your first-year ranking in the second decile reinforced the same message, though it carried less weight. Together, these two early indicators of relative academic standing outweighed every other piece of information.

Your LSAT score of 31 also pushed the prediction toward failure, but its influence was noticeably smaller than your class rankings. While your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 sits almost exactly at the average of accepted students, and your upper-middle family income and full-time study plans are very common among those who were admitted, the model gave these factors little importance compared with your law-school performance ranks.

The system therefore concluded that your academic trajectory in law school made success on the bar exam unlikely. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance, seek targeted bar-preparation support, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise your score meaningfully. These steps would directly address the factors that most influenced the current decision.
